lessons.title: Putting It Together: A Sample Indian Multi-Asset Portfolio Across One Full Cycle

body.text: One portfolio, one real seven-year stretch of Indian market history, every case study from this course in one place. This is what actually applying the framework would have looked like, phase by phase, and roughly how much it would have realistically been worth.

children.text: Start with ₹10 lakh in January 2018 and apply Lesson 1's master allocation table at each phase, using the real events this course has already covered: the IL&FS default, the pre-Covid slowdown, the crash and recovery, the 2022 hiking cycle, and the 2023-24 expansion. This is a simplified, illustrative model built from figures used earlier in this course, not a certified backtest, but it shows the framework in motion rather than in the abstract.
The Walk: Seven Years, Five Phase Calls, One Portfolio

body.title: Applying the framework year by year

events.title: Peak / overheat allocation
events.description: The IL&FS default in September marks the real turn, but the year still calls for a peak-tilted book: broadened equity with a large-cap lean, shortened duration, some gold. The tilt cushions much of the CY2018 smallcap carnage covered in Chapter 2.

events.title: Contraction allocation
events.description: GDP growth confirms the slowdown. Defensive, large-cap-tilted equity, longer duration as the RBI cuts rates through the year, and a bigger gold and cash cushion.

events.title: Trough allocation
events.description: The Covid crash and the sharp recovery both happen within this year. Long duration and gold do their job through the panic and the stimulus-driven rebound that follows.

events.title: Early expansion allocation
events.description: Equity overweight with a cyclical and small/midcap tilt, capturing much of the FY21-style recovery. Gold, true to Chapter 4, is the weakest piece of the book this year.

events.title: Peak / overheat allocation, again
events.description: The full 2022 squeeze: Brent above $120, the RBI's hikes from 4.00% to 6.50%, and rupee depreciation. Shortened duration and a rebuilt gold and cash position soften the blow that hit long-duration bond holders hardest.

events.title: Expansion allocation
events.description: A broad-based domestic recovery, banks, autos, and small/midcaps all contributing, keeps the equity overweight working.

events.title: Expansion, later stage, with caution
events.description: Growth is still positive, but the small/midcap valuation froth and SEBI's stress-test warnings from Chapter 2 argue for trimming into strength rather than adding, exactly the discipline covered in the last lesson.

body.text: Look at where the tilted portfolio actually pulled ahead: mostly in 2021 and 2022 to 2023, not in a single dramatic year, and a meaningful part of the edge came from smaller relative losses during 2018's turbulence rather than spectacular gains anywhere. This matches this course's real lesson: a cycle-aware framework's value shows up gradually, largely through avoiding the worst of a bad phase, not through repeatedly picking the single best trade.

Treat this walk as an illustration of the framework's logic, not a promise of a ~4.6% edge in any future cycle. It uses simplified, rounded, blended returns built from figures already used earlier in this course, ignores the real-world transaction costs and taxes covered in the last lesson, and assumes each year's phase was identified and acted on cleanly, which Chapter 1 already told you is genuinely difficult in real time.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: Which year in this walk applies the same allocation table row as 2022, and why?
options: 2018, because both are peak/overheat allocations tied to a commodity and rate-hiking story
2020, because both involved a market crash
body.explanation: 2018 and 2022 both use the peak/overheat allocation. 2018 came right as the IL&FS default triggered the turn from an overheating economy into contraction, and 2022 was the commodity-price-driven, rate-hiking overheat episode covered across Chapters 1, 3, and 4.

body.title: Reading 2024's Warning Signs
body.scenario: By late 2024, small and midcap valuations are well above historical averages, SEBI's stress-test directive from Chapter 2 is fresh news, and the equity sleeve of your portfolio has grown to be a larger share of your total wealth than your original target, purely from strong 2023 and 2024 gains.
body.prompt: Using everything from this course, what would a disciplined, cycle-aware investor consider doing at this point, and why?
body.modelAnswer: Two separate things are worth doing, and they reinforce each other. First, rebalancing back toward the target allocation, trimming the equity sleeve that has grown oversized purely from its own gains, is a discipline-driven move from the last lesson, not a market call. Second, within the equity sleeve itself, the froth warnings specifically point to trimming the smallcap and midcap overweight built up during the 2023-24 rally, echoing the CY2018 setup, rather than adding further on the strength of recent returns. Neither move requires correctly predicting the next recession; both simply apply the discipline this course has built toward, taking some risk off a book that has run further than its target, right when the evidence says caution is warranted.

children.text: This course opened with a simple claim: every rupee you invest sits inside a bigger machine, the business cycle, and learning to read that machine changes how you think about every asset class you hold. Seven chapters and asset classes later, the walk above is that claim made concrete: the same growth-inflation grid from Chapter 1 explains why equities, bonds, gold, cash, and real estate each took their turn leading and lagging across a real seven-year stretch of Indian market history. You won't call every phase correctly in real time, nobody does, but you now have a framework for reading where the cycle stands, a master allocation table for what to do about it, and a clear-eyed view of the two mistakes, overtrading and performance-chasing, that undo most people who try.

cards.definition: Chapter 1's core framework: mapping rising or falling growth against rising or falling inflation to the asset classes that tend to lead in each combination.
Chapter 2's application of the cycle to equities: cyclicals lead early, commodities lead in overheat, defensives lead in contraction.
Chapter 3's two axes of bond risk: sensitivity to interest rate changes, and sensitivity to a borrower's default risk, each moving differently across the cycle.
Chapter 4's key driver for gold: the nominal rate minus expected inflation, which explains gold's behaviour better than a generic "crisis hedge" story does.
Chapter 5's synthesis: a single table mapping every asset class's typical tilt to each of the four cycle phases, meant to be applied gradually and revisited as evidence accumulates.

body.text: The portfolio walk in this lesson is a simplified, illustrative model built from rounded figures used earlier in this course, not a verified backtest, and it ignores taxes, transaction costs, and the real difficulty of identifying phases in real time. Past patterns, in this walk or anywhere else in this course, do not guarantee future results. Nothing in this course is investment advice; consult a SEBI registered investment adviser to build a portfolio suited to your own goals, horizon, and risk tolerance.

points: Applying the master allocation table across 2018 to 2024, a period covering every major real event used in this course, turned ₹10 lakh into an illustrative ₹22.85 lakh, versus ₹21.84 lakh for a never-tilted static neutral mix
The edge from tilting was real but modest, about ₹1.01 lakh or 4.6% over seven years, and came mostly from smaller relative losses in the 2018-19 turbulence rather than one spectacular year
This walk is an illustration of the framework's logic using this course's own rounded figures, not a certified backtest or a promise of any specific future edge
Late 2024's froth warnings called for the same discipline as the last lesson: rebalancing an oversized equity sleeve and trimming small/midcap exposure into strength, not predicting the next downturn

The core idea threading through all five chapters is the one this course opened with: every asset class you hold sits inside the same growth-inflation machine, and reading that machine, imperfectly but consistently, is worth more than any single hot tip
